detail.abstract: Young urban Indians aged 18–34 constitute the core buyer for India’s mid-range smartphone segment, yet the feature-level pricing dynamics that govern their purchase decisions remain empirically underexamined. This study examines feature-specific price sensitivity and its demographic moderators among this population in the Rs.15,000 segment, applying a principal-agent framework to predict how payment structure shapes price responsiveness. A purposive sample of 127 young urban Indian consumers evaluated five feature upgrades — storage, camera, random access memory, charging speed, and battery life — at two price points. Storage attracted the strongest baseline preference and the lowest price sensitivity; battery life attracted the weakest preference and the highest sensitivity. The feature hierarchy was statistically significant and demographically invariant across all tested buyer groups. Consistent with principal-agent predictions, parent-funded buyers exhibited twice the composite price sensitivity of self-funders, and buyers aged 18–24 were more sensitive than the 25–34 cohort. These two effects share substantial variance, suggesting they co-express a latent construct of parental financial dependence rather than independent mechanisms. Gender, income, and usage intensity returned null results. Across demographic groups, what varies is not which features are valued but how acutely price resistance manifests when upgrades must be justified to a third-party funder.

title: Commitment Under Uncertainty: A Costly Signaling Approach
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Commitment Under Uncertainty: A Costly Signaling Approach
detail.abstract: Early relationships involve extreme information asymmetry. Most available signals-words, gestures, emotional expressions-are cheap to produce. Costly signaling theory suggests that actions carrying real personal cost might reveal more. This paper outlines a behavioral observation approach built around temporal compression: creating a short window where stated commitments must turn into observable behavior. Under that pressure, several patterns tend to surface. Polished self-presentation frays. Boundary conversations get reframed away from the original issue. Strong early compliance sometimes gives way to gradual disengagement. And the observer's own sunk costs can start driving the decision. A tiny pilot log (N=35, eight weeks) found that people whose relationships dissolved tended to have lower follow-through and declining consistency trends. That's just a description of a convenience sample-nothing more. The approach is provisional and keeps changing.

detail.abstract: Modeling user psychological states in digital health faces challenges regarding irregular time intervals and dynamic resistance to interventions. Existing discrete models distort dynamics, while black-box differential equations fail to isolate causal effects. We propose GC-NODE (Gated Controlled Neural ODE), a continuous-time framework modeling psychological evolution as a controlled differential equation. It employs a structural decoupling mechanism to explicitly separate system dynamics into endogenous drift, exogenous control, and statedependent resistance gating. This physically constrained architecture improves prediction accuracy on irregular time series and enables the inference of dynamic resistance curves and counterfactual trajectory deduction. Experiments on large-scale panel data demonstrate that GC-NODE outperforms baselines in prediction and interpretability, providing a theoretical basis for personalized intelligent interventions.

detail.title: Public Support for Reparameterization: An Information Experiment on Entrenched Fiscal Rules in an Aging Society

publicationDetails.detailsText: KDI School of Pub Policy & Management Paper No. WP26-12

detail.abstract: As aging societies face rising claims on public budgets, governments increasingly confront the question of whether to reparameterize statutory fiscal rules. We use a nationally representative survey experiment with 3,066 Korean adults to test whether concise information can shift public support both for overall education-spending levels and for the underlying allocation rule: Korea's Local Education Finance Grant, which statutorily earmarks 20.79% of internal tax revenue. Three information treatments, emphasizing expenditure efficiency under demographic change, international benchmarks, and cross-sector budget trade-offs, each lower the preferred education share by 2-3 percentage points. The efficiency and reference-point treatments also raise support for replacing the fixed earmark with a demographically linked rule by 5-7 percentage points. Belief updating is strongest among respondents previously unaware of the formula; parents revise their assessments of spending adequacy but resist structural rule reform. The findings suggest that targeted information can build public constituencies for reparameterization, not just retrenchment, of entrenched fiscal rules, a margin that is likely to matter in other aging economies with rigid statutory earmarks.

title: Bayesian Time-Varying Meta-Analysis via Hierarchical Mean-Variance Random-effects Models
affiliations: NTT DOCOMO, INC., Keio University, Yokohama City University and Keio University

detail.title: Bayesian Time-Varying Meta-Analysis via Hierarchical Mean-Variance Random-effects Models
detail.abstract: Meta-analysis is widely used to integrate results from multiple experiments to obtain generalized insights. Since meta-analysis datasets are often heteroscedastic due to varying subgroups and temporal heterogeneity arising from experiments conducted at different time points, the typical meta-analysis approach, which assumes homoscedasticity, fails to adequately address this heteroscedasticity among experiments. This paper proposes a new Bayesian estimation method that simultaneously shrinks estimates of the means and variances of experiments using a hierarchical Bayesian approach while accounting for time effects through a Gaussian process. This method connects experiments via the hierarchical framework, enabling "borrowing strength" between experiments to achieve high-precision estimates of each experiment's mean. The method can flexibly capture potential time trends in datasets by modeling time effects with the Gaussian process. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method through simulation studies and illustrate its practical utility using a real marketing promotions dataset.

title: EnduranceNet: an EfficientNet-based dual-branch network with Efficient Channel Attention for robust brain tumor classification from MRI scans
affiliations: Kanazawa University, Kanazawa University, Telkom University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Kanazawa University

detail.title: EnduranceNet: an EfficientNet-based dual-branch network with Efficient Channel Attention for robust brain tumor classification from MRI scans
detail.abstract: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a challenging task due to data scarcity, class imbalance, and variability in tumor appearance. Limited interpretability of deep learning models further hinders their adoption in clinical practice, where transparency and trust are critical. Existing approaches often rely on extensive data augmentation or computationally intensive architectures, which reduce practicality in resource-constrained settings. To address these challenges, we propose EnduranceNet, a lightweight dual-branch architecture for robust multiclass brain tumor classification under distribution shifts and heterogeneous tumor characteristics. The model integrates parallel fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 and EfficientNetB1 backbones to capture complementary feature representations. An Efficient Channel Attention (ECA) module enhances channel-wise feature selectivity, while focal loss mitigates class imbalance. Experiments on the Kaggle Brain MRI dataset (7,023 samples) evaluated performance using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, with comparisons to state-of-the-art methods and computational efficiency analysis. EnduranceNet achieved 99.29% accuracy, 99.25% precision, 99.24% recall, and 99.24% F1-score with 12.43 million parameters and 2.11 G-FLOPs. The model remained robust under reduced training data and noisy test conditions. Additional evaluation on the BRISC dataset (6,000 MRI samples) confirmed generalization under distribution shifts. Beyond performance, the model provides Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)-based visual explanations that highlight tumor-relevant regions, supporting transparent and clinically meaningful interpretation. Overall, EnduranceNet offers an effective balance between accuracy, efficiency, robustness, and interpretability for trustworthy computer-aided diagnosis.

title: Beyond the Firm: A Cross-Border Saudization Index (CBSI) for Measuring Localization Impact in Saudi Arabia's Digital Economy
affiliations: Golden Gate University

detail.title: Beyond the Firm: A Cross-Border Saudization Index (CBSI) for Measuring Localization Impact in Saudi Arabia's Digital Economy
detail.abstract: Saudi Arabia's Saudization policy has delivered measurable labor market gains under Vision 2030, reducing unemployment and expanding private-sector participation. However, the rapid growth of the digital economynow estimated at approximately 15.6 percent of GDPand the emergence of crossborder platforms as major intermediaries in retail, logistics, and services have exposed a structural gap in existing localization instruments. Current frameworks, centered on the Nitaqat system, measure the share of Saudi nationals within resident firms but do not systematically capture the localization footprint of cross-border and digitally intensive firms that capture significant Saudi demand without a commensurate domestic operational presence. This paper proposes the Cross-Border Saudization Index (CBSI), a conceptual composite index designed to measure the contribution of cross-border firms to the Saudi economy relative to their market capture. CBSI is structured around five theoretically grounded dimensions: Saudi Job Intensity (30%), Local Operations Depth (20%), Local Value Retention (20%), SME Linkages (15%), and Knowledge Transfer and Senior Jobs (15%). Drawing on global value chain theory, local content policy literature, and regulatory arbitrage scholarship, the paper develops the framework, justifies its structure, and proposes a Delphi-based validation study as the next empirical step. The findings suggest that CBSI can complement existing Saudization instruments by extending localization scrutiny to cross-border actors, supporting a more competitive-neutral regulatory environment, and reinforcing Saudi Arabia's capacity to capture higher-value activities from the growing digital economy.

title: Technical Efficiency in Informal-Sector Manufacturing Enterprises in India: Analysis of Determinants of Technical Efficiency with a Special Focus on Female-Owned Enterprises
affiliations: Institute of Economic Growth (IEG)

detail.title: Technical Efficiency in Informal-Sector Manufacturing Enterprises in India: Analysis of Determinants of Technical Efficiency with a Special Focus on Female-Owned Enterprises
detail.abstract: Using unit-level data of the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), 2022-23, technical efficiency in India's informal sector (alternatively called unorganized sector) manufacturing enterprises is estimated and studied. A stochastic frontier production (value-added) function, coupled with a technical inefficiency model, is estimated using data on about 108,000 manufacturing enterprises. The mean technical efficiency is found to be about 60% lower for female-owned enterprises than for male-owned enterprises among own-account enterprises (OAEs), which do not have any hired workers, and about 20% lower among hired-worker enterprises (HWEs) --the efficiency gap between male-and female-headed enterprises being substantially lower among HWEs than among OAEs. The results of the analysis suggest that if a home-based, own-account female-headed manufacturing enterprise gets transformed (with policy support) into a more formalized enterprise with hired workers and a location outside the household premises (which typically involves scaling up the business), there will be an increase in the technical efficiency of the female-owned enterprise, i.e., the productivity disadvantage will be lowered. The results indicate that entrepreneurial education and improved access to credit will also help raise the technical efficiency of female-headed enterprises.

title: Can Trade-Climate Transitions Fail Operationally? Institutional Congestion Risk in Export-Dependent Economies

detail.title: Can Trade-Climate Transitions Fail Operationally? Institutional Congestion Risk in Export-Dependent Economies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, personal data collection, or experimental procedures requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Trade-climate transitions are rapidly reshaping development policy, export competitiveness and climate governance across emerging economies. Governments are simultaneously expanding climate-related trade measures, ESG reporting systems, traceability requirements, customs modernization, certification infrastructures, and digitally interconnected compliance architectures.

Existing transition frameworks largely assume that implementation success depends primarily upon financing availability, political commitment or aggregate institutional capacity. This paper argues that transitions may also fail through a less visible mechanism: operational congestion within strategically central implementation systems.

Building upon the Institutional Threshold Capacity (ITC) framework developed in earlier research, the paper introduces the concept of institutional congestion risk: the accumulation of overlapping implementation pressures upon customs systems, certification agencies, laboratories, interoperability architectures and cross-agency coordination mechanisms simultaneously.

The paper argues that modern trade-climate transitions increasingly generate hidden operational concentration dynamics because multiple governance architectures progressively converge upon the same institutional infrastructures at the same time. Under such conditions, transition fragility may emerge not from policy failure in principle, but from implementation saturation in practice.

Particular attention is devoted to export-dependent and emerging economies where customs systems, standards agencies, conformity-assessment infrastructures and digital coordination mechanisms increasingly operate as critical operational gateways for climate-compatible trade integration.

The paper further develops a systems-diagnostics framework for identifying hidden implementation congestion before wider dysfunction becomes externally visible. It proposes approaches for measuring institutional absorption pressure, detecting operational dependency concentration, stress-testing strategically central systems, and designing congestion-aware transition governance frameworks.

The study contributes to emerging debates on trade-climate governance, institutional resilience and transition management by shifting analytical attention from aggregate transition ambition toward the operational absorption dynamics that increasingly determine implementation viability under expanding governance complexity.

title: Three Kinds of Trust, and the Slide Between Them A Trust Taxonomy for Human-AI Co-Existence
affiliations: and Chiang Mai University

detail.title: Three Kinds of Trust, and the Slide Between Them A Trust Taxonomy for Human-AI Co-Existence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no
declarations.funderStatement: self funded

detail.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence is widely discussed as a quantity to be calibrated, yet the calibration literature treats trust as scalar: a gap between a user's reliance and a system's reliability, to be narrowed by correcting over-trust and under-trust. This paper argues that trust in large language models is better understood as three distinct relations; operational trust in competence, epistemic trust in truthfulness, and emotional trust in safety, that operate on different evidence, carry different risks, and fail in different ways. In human relationships these three dimensions are correlated, and generalizing across them is adaptive: a person who is demonstrably competent is, on average, also more likely to be honest and to mean us well. Large language models decouple them. They are broadly competent, unreliably accurate, and constitutively incapable of care. The result is a directional and ordered failure we name the trust leak: warranted operational trust silently inflates epistemic trust, which in turn inflates.

title: Nifty 50 Index Put Option Mispricing: A BCJ-Style Test 2015–2025

detail.title: Nifty 50 Index Put Option Mispricing: A BCJ-Style Test 2015–2025
detail.abstract: Equity index put options in the United States have long earned returns too negative to be reconciled with standard asset-pricing models, a puzzle first formally quantified by Broadie, Chernov, and Johannes (2009), hereafter BCJ, using finite-sample Monte Carlo inference on S&P 500 data. This paper asks whether the same anomaly exists in India. We apply the BCJ finite-sample simulation framework to Nifty 50 index put options over January 2015 to April 2025, a 119-month sample spanning the 2018 NBFC credit stress, the COVID-19 dislocation of 2020, and the 2022 global inflation and rate-hike cycle. Three structural models are estimated from Nifty 50 daily returns: Black-Scholes (BS), Heston (1993) stochastic volatility (SV), and Bates (1996, 2000) stochastic volatility with jumps (SVJ), with SV parameters obtained via Markov chain Monte Carlo and SVJ parameters via method of moments (the SVJ MCMC chains did not fully converge; SVJ results are therefore reported as a robustness check on the SV findings). For each model we generate 25,000 simulated return paths and compute finite-sample p-values for held-to-maturity put returns across four moneyness buckets. Delta-neutral strategies, the ATM straddle and crash-neutral spread, reject the no-additional-risk-premium null at p = 0.000 under all three models, a result that survives both jump-risk (γ = 10) and estimation-risk adjustments to the risk-neutral measure. Regime analysis shows that the variance risk premium strengthens monotonically across successive stress episodes and does not revert to pre-2018 levels. Our results suggest that tail-risk protection is priced more expensively in Indian equity options than in the U.S., with implications for hedging strategy and options market structure in emerging-market derivatives.

title: Tackling Hidden Retaliation for Strike Participation: Examples of Legal Protection from Detriments Short of Dismissal
affiliations: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI), University of Kassel - Universität Kassel, University of Barcelona, CY Cergy Paris Université, Catholic University of Louvain (UCL), Kristianstad University, University of Osijek, University of Southern Denmark and Catholic University of Portugal (UCP)

detail.title: Tackling Hidden Retaliation for Strike Participation: Examples of Legal Protection from Detriments Short of Dismissal

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
For workers, employer retaliation represents a major threat in response to their participation in a strike. While dismissal is the most visible form of such retaliation, it can also take more ‘hidden’ forms, such as demotion, disciplinary sanctions or withdrawal of voluntary overtime. Addressing a notable gap, protections from detriments short of dismissal are expected to be introduced into UK law by the soon to be enacted Employment Rights Act. The purpose of this brief is to situate the United Kingdom (UK) within a broader set of comparative examples of how the law protects workers from detriments short of dismissal for participation in a lawful strike in eight other European countries (Belgium, Croatia, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain and Sweden). 

The analysis produces several key findings of relevance to policymakers:

 • The legal framework should make sure that it considers all the different dimensions of protection to ensure solid and broad legal protection as gaps in one area can undermine the entire system. 
• Countries with broad protection typically rely on open-ended legal norms, such as prohibiting all acts ‘harming’ or ‘discriminating’ against workers or barring any ‘other prejudicial treatment’, rather than a closed list enumerating all prohibited detriments.
• Proving the link between a detriment and strike participation can be difficult for a worker, especially if the test is highly restrictive. To address this, many countries provide for a reversal of the burden of proof and legal presumptions favouring workers.
• Most countries offer a broad range of remedies, combining nonmonetary and monetary remedies.
• The law in most countries makes it possible for trade unions to bring claims for detriment short of dismissal, in addition and/or behalf of affected workers, acknowledging the collective harms of such detriments and the risk of individual workers' reluctance to take legal action due to fear of job loss.

title: Complex Modern Portfolio Theory
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School - Department of Finance, Yale University, Yale SOM and Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne

detail.title: Complex Modern Portfolio Theory
detail.abstract:
The literature has long wrestled with the practical usefulness of Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT), and extensive evidence shows its performance decreases rapidly with the number of assets (N ). We present several new and counterintuitive facts about MPT. Most importantly, the performance of MPT in fact increases with N once the number of assets exceeds the number of training observations (T ). This finding holds in a variety of settings: in conjunction with popular portfolio regularization methods, in a variety of asset universes, and when T is large or small.

title: Sticky Rents: A Simple Implicit-Contracts Theory

detail.title: Sticky Rents: A Simple Implicit-Contracts Theory

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Cleveland Working Paper No. 26-12
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Shelter inflation, driven by continuing-tenant rents, accounts for one-third of the consumer price index (CPI). Yet continuing-tenant rent inflation, notoriously sticky, has attracted almost no theoretical attention. Standard sticky price theories cannot explain the basic facts. We provide a simple theory yielding implicit contracts as an equilibrium. The landlord will wish to renege when costs rise; reputation is unavailable to enforce the contract. A well-established mechanism serves: landlord off-equilibrium-path play might result in renter frustration and endogenous breakup. Our implicit-contracts theory gracefully explains nominal (rather than real) rigidity, and provides a microfounded explanation of key rental market facts.

title: Who Supports a (just) Green Transition? Eco-Social Divides and Public Opinion Towards Green and Social Policies in Europe
affiliations: University of Milan and Politecnico di Milano School of Management

detail.title: Who Supports a (just) Green Transition? Eco-Social Divides and Public Opinion Towards Green and Social Policies in Europe

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The European Green Deal has fuelled a political backlash against EU climate policies, strengthening Eurosceptic parties. This backlash reflects politically sensitive tensions inherent in the trade-offs between environmental protection, economic growth, and social inclusion. 

Against this backdrop, this paper asks: who feels threatened by the green transition? Do workers and occupational groups differ in their support for environmental and social policies? And does support increase when environmental sustainability is combined with social protection? 

We address these questions using original public opinion data collected at the University of Milan (Ferrera et al. 2022), which distinguish preferences across different types of policies: social protection and social investment, as well as green taxes, subsidies, and regulations. 

Our findings are threefold. 

First, we identify a widespread perception of socio-ecological risk linked to the unintended consequences of climate policies. Concerns about job losses associated with the green transition are highly salient across countries, particularly among lower-income and less-educated individuals, and among precarious segments of the labour market. 

Second, our analysis refines our understanding of eco-social divides in relation to specific policy types: social (protection) policies find broad support among vulnerable groups, whereas green taxes emerge as the least popular measure. Interestingly, however, some occupational groups — not only those better positioned in the labour market — show support for both social and environmental policies. 

Third, our results suggest that combining environmental and compensatory measures such as support for workers and wealth taxes can help broaden public backing for a just green transition, mitigating perceived trade-offs and distributional conflicts.

title: State-Mediated Structural Injustice
affiliations: University College London - Faculty of Laws

detail.title: State-Mediated Structural Injustice

publicationDetails.detailsText: Faculty of Laws University College London Law Research Paper No. 15/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: University College London Faculty of Laws Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in C Cordelli (ed), Structural Injustice, NOMOS: Yearbook of the American Society for Political and Legal Philosophy, New York University Press, 2027

detail.abstract: In her account of structural injustice, Iris Marion Young illustrates the concept with the story of Sandy.  Sandy is a single mother of two who finds herself on the verge of homelessness as a result of everyday circumstances associated with a market economy and changing patterns of property use and development. All individuals with whom Sandy interacted, such as landlords and estate agents, acted according to the law and treated her with decency. However, Sandy suffers an injustice in Young’s view, as no one should be in a position of deep housing insecurity, particularly in an affluent society in which others benefit from the practices that led to her predicament. Young developed the concept to describe situations where people find themselves suffering serious harm, such as exploitation and domination, which is neither through their own fault nor intentionally caused by one individual or institution. It occurs when individuals act according to normal rules and morally justifiable practices, but the preconditions and results of their actions are structural processes that produce unjust outcomes.  Considering who is responsible for this, Young explains that multiple factors come together to cause the situation, and no individual or company or law can be singled out as a major factor. In a case such as this, it is hard to ascribe what Young describes as backward-looking responsibility, to know what can be done, and who has the power to do it. Structural injustice is different from injustice perpetuated by individuals, by the state, or by other powerful institutions.

title: The Time for a Coherent and Binding EU Approach to Psychosocial Risk Prevention is Now
affiliations: Lancaster University, Nottingham University Business School, European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) and European Trade Union Institute (ETUI)

detail.title: The Time for a Coherent and Binding EU Approach to Psychosocial Risk Prevention is Now

publicationDetails.journalName: European Trade Union Institute (ETUI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
– Psychosocial risks at work constitute a major and growing occupational health problem. Almost 45% of workers in the EU report being exposed to risks at work that could negatively affect their mental health, and almost one-third experience stress, depression or anxiety linked to work.

– The European Union’s (EU) legislation on occupational safety and health (OSH) requires protection from all work-related risks, but fails explicitly to define and regulate psychosocial risks at work.

– In the absence of clear legal obligations, prevention efforts remain misdirected towards individuals rather than work organisation, design and management, which contradicts the OSH hierarchy of prevention and control measures.

– Political, institutional, and scientific evidence now converges on the need for clear and binding EU action on psychosocial risks at work. Fragmented and inconsistent references across EU and national legislation generate legal uncertainty, weaken enforcement, and result in uneven levels of worker protection. National diversity in OSH systems further strengthens the case for a harmonised EU framework establishing minimum enforceable standards, while allowing national systems and social partners to build on them.

Key points

title: Programmable Re-Coupling: Monetary Policy Transmission and the Design of Central Bank Digital Currency

detail.title: Programmable Re-Coupling: Monetary Policy Transmission and the Design of Central Bank Digital Currency

detail.abstract: The transition from physical cash to digital payments has weakened the behavioural channel through which monetary policy transmits to household spending decisions. This paper formalises this degradation through the Coupling Coefficient (Φ ∈ [0,1]), a parameter measuring the alignment between central bank policy intent and realised household-level response. I show that standard digital payment systems (exemplified by India's Unified Payments Interface) operate at low Φ because they eliminate the cognitive friction-the "pain of paying"-that physical cash provided automatically. A Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) with activated programmability features (remuneration, purpose-binding, and calibrated cognitive friction) can restore and potentially exceed the coupling efficiency of cash. I derive the Programmable Re-Coupling Hypothesis: ΦCBDC > Φcash > ΦUPI, subject to scope conditions in welfare transfer contexts. Using India's e-Rupee pilot as the primary case study, and drawing on the Bank for International Settlements' CBDC research framework for cross-jurisdictional context, I analyse the design parameters that determine a CBDC's monetary policy impact. The analysis identifies a structural tension: the features that strengthen transmission (remuneration, programmability) are precisely those that threaten financial stability through bank disintermediation. I propose an optimal design space that calibrates CBDC adoption to maintain financial stability while enabling targeted policy transmission, and derive three testable empirical propositions for household behaviour under programmable CBDC regimes.

title: When Execution Becomes Cheap Evaluative Capacity, Problem-Selection Judgment, and the Dual Threshold Trap

detail.title: When Execution Becomes Cheap Evaluative Capacity, Problem-Selection Judgment, and the Dual Threshold Trap
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence creates a two-dimensional knowledge problem for entrepreneurs: evaluative capacity θₑ, the ability to detect and correct AI errors, and problem-selection judgment θₛ, the ability to identify which problems have genuine value. Execution skill is respecified as σᵢ(A), a task-specific function of AI capability: as A grows, σ differences across workers converge to zero and the threshold surface in (θₑ, θₛ) space becomes the primary determinant of productivity differences. A dynamic accumulation equation with full derivation shows that market contact raises θₛ faster than θₑ, because real feedback is precise about value in ways that formal study cannot replicate. Three results follow. First, AI compresses execution differences: σ₀ becomes a progressively weaker predictor of output as A grows, and the threshold surface in (θₑ, θₛ) space becomes the primary determinant of entrepreneurial productivity. Second, the dual threshold trap-technically competent founders who misdirect AI effort toward low-value problems-generates an opportunity cost that increases with AI capability under fixed threshold structure, and this result is robust to concave AI leverage. Third, market contact is the efficient escape route from the trap: the ratio βₛ/αₛ quantifies how much faster customer exposure reduces threshold-crossing time than equivalent internal study.

title: Externalized Cooperation and Institutional Continuity: Records, Inheritance, and Legal Personhood as Institutional Mechanisms

detail.title: Externalized Cooperation and Institutional Continuity: Records, Inheritance, and Legal Personhood as Institutional Mechanisms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no competing financial interests, personal relationships, institutional affiliations, or external funding sources that could have influenced the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because the paper is a theoretical work and does not involve human participants, patient data, experiments, surveys, interviews, or identifiable personal information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract:
Institutional economics, property-rights theory, incomplete-contract theory, organizational law and economics, and organizational-capital research have shown how institutions reduce transaction costs, stabilize property-rights expectations, constrain opportunism, support long-term investment, and sustain organizational continuity. This paper introduces a narrower question: when the natural person who carries memory, control, authority, or liability permanently exits the bargaining, interpretive, performance, and enforcement space, how can facts, resource control, and organizational commitments remain effective? The paper calls this the post-mortem commitment continuity problem.

Within the Mortality Economics framework, the paper distinguishes three forms of post-mortem cooperative rupture: factual rupture, resource-control rupture, and commitment-subject rupture. Records, accounts, archives, and registration externalize facts; property rights, inheritance, wills, and trusts externalize resource control; contracts, courts, legal personhood, and offices externalize commitment content, enforcement procedures, and commitment subjects. The central proposition is that one deep economic function of historical institutions is not merely to reduce transaction costs among the living, but to make cooperative structures preservable, transferable, enforceable, inheritable, and reconnectable after the death of natural persons.

To make the argument economically tractable, the paper proposes a minimal formal model in which post-mortem cooperative continuity depends on record quality R, property and inheritance externalization I, legal enforceability L, legal-personhood continuity J, personal dependence P_dep, and externalization quality Q. This model is linked to C_v = φ_t · S_t · Q_ext,t, where φ_t denotes the externalization rate, S_t denotes the accumulated historical stock of externalized cooperation, and Q_ext,t denotes externalization quality. Legal personhood is interpreted as an advanced integrative form of C_ext: contracts preserve commitment content, courts preserve enforcement procedures, while legal personhood preserves the commitment subject itself.

The paper also reinterprets the legal problem of dead-hand control as dead-hand continuity within Mortality Economics: institutional arrangements without sufficient updating, accountability, or exit mechanisms may preserve control, privilege, monopoly, and liability avoidance rather than productive cooperation. The paper develops four empirical strategies: record-reform designs, inheritance and property-law reform designs, key-person sudden-death event studies, and panel or event-study designs for dead-hand control structures. It thus moves Mortality Economics from abstract mechanism toward an institutional analysis amenable to modeling, estimation, and falsification.

title: Deep Learning-Based Attention-Guided Framework for Multi-Source Diabetic Retinopathy Screening
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Deep Learning-Based Attention-Guided Framework for Multi-Source Diabetic Retinopathy Screening
detail.abstract: Diabetic Retinopathy is a leading cause of preventable blindness, and early detection is critical for timely clinical intervention. Traditional screening depends on specialist evaluation and dedicated imaging infrastructure, limiting accessibility in resource-constrained regions. This study presents an automated deep learning-based DR grading system developed using large-scale retinal fundus data. The proposed model is built upon the EfficientNet-B3 architecture integrated with an Efficient Channel Attention(ECA) module to enhance feature representation. Training was performed on a unified multi-dataset comprising 92,501 originalimages sourced from the EyePACS, APTOS, and Messidor databases, which was further expanded to 143,669 images through standardized augmentation provided by the dataset authors. This multi-dataset training strategy exposes the model to heterogeneous imaging conditions, improving robustness across diverse clinical settings. A comprehensive preprocessing pipeline-including CLAHE, gamma correction, and advanced augmentation was applied to enhance retinal structures and reduce overfitting. Label smoothing, class reweighting, and Cut Mix were incorporated to mitigate class imbalance. Model development and optimization were carried out on NVIDIA Tesla P100 GPUs using mixed-precision training for efficiency. Performance was evaluated through stratified 3-fold cross validation on the full 143,669-image pool with a held-out 10% test set of 14,367 images. The final ensemble model achieved an overall accuracy of 88.6%, a Quadratic Weighted Kappa score of 0.917, and a weighted F1-score of 0.883. These results demonstrate that an efficient and lightweight attention-enhanced CNN can serve as a reliable and scalable tool for automated DR screening, with strong potential for real time deployment in teleophthalmology and resource constrained clinical environments.

title: Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models
affiliations: Yale SOM, Ecole Polytechnique Federale de Lausanne, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) and AQR Capital Management, LLC

detail.title: Scaling Point-in-Time Language Models
detail.abstract:
Large language models trained on unrestricted internet corpora inevitably embed information from the future, introducing lookahead bias that compromises the validity of backtests and causal inference in finance and the social sciences. Point-in-time language models—trained exclusively on text available up to each calendar date—eliminate this leakage by construction, but existing efforts typically produce models that lag substantially behind their unconstrained counterparts. We show that this performance gap can be narrowed through scale. Training decoder-only transformers with up to 4 billion parameters on 1 trillion chronologically filtered tokens from FineWeb, we construct a sequence of monthly model checkpoints spanning 2013–2024. Across a range of common-sense reasoning and language understanding benchmarks, our models approach the performance of leading open-weight models of comparable size (such as Gemma-3-4B and LLaMA-7B) trained on temporally unrestricted data, although a performance gap remains on several tasks. Finally, in a strict out-of-sample economic evaluation task, portfolios built from point-in-time embeddings achieve robust positive Sharpe ratios and perform close to full-sample counterparts that violate temporal validity, indicating that chronologically consistent language models can extract economically meaningful signals without relying on look-ahead bias. We release the complete pipeline—including dataset construction, training infrastructure, and evaluation code—to enable reproducible point-in-time language modeling and to support research applications that require strict temporal validity.

title: Money Laundering, Digital Currencies, and the Problem of Visibility Making P2P Networks and Other Technologies Visible in Law
affiliations: and

detail.title: Money Laundering, Digital Currencies, and the Problem of Visibility Making P2P Networks and Other Technologies Visible in Law
detail.abstract: This article argues that money laundering through digital currencies presents not simply a novel compliance challenge, but a deeper problem of legal visibility in transnational financial governance. Digital assets do not render anti-money laundering (AML) law obsolete; rather, they expose a structural weakness long embedded in the international legal order. While value now moves through borderless, instantaneous, and technically complex infrastructures, states continue to govern financial crime through territorially bounded institutions and unevenly coordinated legal mechanisms. The core difficulty, the article contends, is not anonymity alone. It is that legal visibility depends on a fragile chain of translation: from wallet to person, transaction to evidence, platform to jurisdiction, and suspicion to seizure. Each link in that chain remains vulnerable to divergence, delay, and institutional refusal. Against the familiar claim that law merely "lags" technological innovation, the article develops a critical account of digital-currency laundering as a stress test for the existing AML regime. It shows that the current framework is not a legal vacuum, but a layered assemblage of treaty obligations, FATF standards, domestic implementation, private gatekeeping, and increasingly data-intensive supervisory practices. Yet this architecture remains structurally ill-suited to digital assets because traceability is too often mistaken for governability. Blockchain systems may preserve abundant data, but data do not identify legal subjects or generate lawful authority by themselves; they must be translated through exchanges, analytics firms, subpoenas, mutual legal assistance channels, and evidentiary standards before law can act. The article proceeds in five parts. It first defines digital-currency laundering and situates it within a broader genealogy of AML as a mode of transnational governance. It then examines the doctrinal architecture of the international AML order and explains why it fails in the digital setting, before analyzing the invisibility problem, the political economy of seizure and cooperation, and the limits of managerial reform. The argument is then developed through the Asia-Pacific region as a structural case study, through an account of "machine lawyering" and the production of evidentiary visibility, and finally through the HankoTrade model as an illustration of how custody, value transmission, and platform design fragment legal responsibility. The article concludes that the relevant task is not to maximize transparency, but to build forms of legitimate visibility that are reviewable, proportionate, and institutionally supportable across jurisdictions.

title: Comparative Assessment of Case Definitions on the Epidemiology of Asymptomatic Pulmonary Tuberculosis in China: A Nationwide Surveillance Analysis, 2021–2024

detail.title: Comparative Assessment of Case Definitions on the Epidemiology of Asymptomatic Pulmonary Tuberculosis in China: A Nationwide Surveillance Analysis, 2021–2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: Funded by the National Science and Technology Major Project (2025ZD01901000) and the National TB Control Project, China CDC (261103-2026).

detail.abstract:
Background: The proportion and epidemiological profile of asymptomatic tuberculosis (TB) vary widely depending on symptom criteria, yet no standardized case definition exists. Understanding how definitional differences impact surveillance estimates and risk factor associations is critical for accurate burden assessment and targeted intervention. This study compares two common symptom-based definitions of asymptomatic TB and evaluates their influence on estimated prevalence, risk factor associations, temporal trends, and geographic distribution in China.

Methods: We analyzed national TB surveillance data (January 2021–December 2024, n=1,037,934). Asymptomatic TB was defined as: D1: absence of all TB-related symptoms; D2: absence of cough, expectoration, or hemoptysis. We compared case proportions (McNemar’s test), assessed risk factors (logistic regression), and analyzed temporal and spatial trends (segmented regression and geographic mapping).

Findings: D2 identified nearly twice as many asymptomatic cases as D1 (14.74% vs. 8.29%, difference +6.45%, p<0.001), reclassifying 67,022 (6.5%). Risk factor associations were attenuated under D2: odds ratios for 41/46 subgroups shifted toward 1.0, reducing discriminative power. Temporal trends showed a national peak in early 2022 then decline, with marked provincial heterogeneity. Geographic disparities were more pronounced under D1, revealing a strong south-to-north gradient.

Interpretation: Asymptomatic TB definition choice affects epidemiological estimates, risk factor identification, and geographic patterns. The stricter definition (D1) better captures screening-relevant populations and should be considered for standardizing surveillance and guiding active case-finding in high-burden settings.

title: Fiscal Rules, Agribusiness Booms, and Agricultural Frontier Municipalities: Causal Evidence from Brazil
affiliations: Universidade do Estado de Mato Grosso and UFMS

detail.title: Fiscal Rules, Agribusiness Booms, and Agricultural Frontier Municipalities: Causal Evidence from Brazil
detail.abstract: Brazil enacted Complementary Law No. 173/2020 (LC 173) at the height of the pandemic fiscal crisis, handing municipalities R$60 billion in emergency transfers while simultaneously restricting personnel expenditures for those whose payrollto-revenue ratio had exceeded 0.58 in 2019. We examine 3,445 municipalities over 2017-2023 to understand what those two simultaneous moves produced. On own-source tax revenue, the Synthetic DiD estimator (Arkhangelsky et al., 2021) shows that municipalities under the Article 8 restrictions raised their own-source collection by +9.7% relative to comparable municipalities that narrowly escaped the threshold (τ SDID = +0.092, p = 0.003). The Legal Amazon goes further: +32.7% (τ SDID = +0.283, p = 0.007). That gap between the national and frontier estimates is the paper's core finding. Frontier municipalities had a large latent tax base-ISS on agro-logistics, ITBI on heated land markets, IPTU on appreciated urban real estate-generated by the simultaneous soybean supercycle. The fiscal rule gave them reason to mobilize it. A Bartik instrument confirms that the commodity boom alone, without the rule, generated zero additional own-source revenue in soybean-producing municipalities. On personnel expenditure, treated municipalities reduced their DTP/RCL ratio by 2.9-4.1 percentage points for Brazil and 4.0 points for the Amazon. More remarkably, the gap kept widening after Article 8 expired in late 2021. By 2023, the Callaway-Sant'Anna event study records-7.0 pp for Brazil-more than double the initial impact. A fiscal rule that lasted eighteen months changed how municipal administrators think about payroll for at least four years afterward.

title: What is the Impact of Educational Spending on Short and Long Term Outcomes? Evidence from Colombia

detail.title: What is the Impact of Educational Spending on Short and Long Term Outcomes? Evidence from Colombia
detail.abstract: Two-thirds of low-and middle-income countries are planning cuts to education spending following the global pandemic. This paper exploits two sources of plausibly exogenous variation in education spending in Colombia. I leverage the 2011 constitutional repeal that removed elevated education funding from oil-producing municipalities. Using individual-level high school exit exam data from more than one million students, I find a 25 percent cut in per-pupil expenditure reduces language scores by 0.05 standard deviations and math scores by 0.04 standard deviations. Students affected are 2.5 percentage points less likely to graduate from university. Learning losses are 2-3 times larger for low-income students, students with less-educated parents, and females. I then instrument per-pupil spending with international oil prices and find that short-term increases raise the high school graduation rate by 8 percent.

title: The Uncounted: A Case for Federal Enumeration of the Bereaved Parent Demographic in the United States

detail.title: The Uncounted: A Case for Federal Enumeration of the Bereaved Parent Demographic in the United States

detail.abstract: The National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), as the designated federal statistical agency for health data under Section 306 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 242k), collects, analyzes, and disseminates mortality data on the population of the United States. The existing data infrastructure documents the deceased: cause of death, age, sex, race, ethnicity, and geography. It does not enumerate the surviving parent population-the bereaved parents who outlive their children and who carry documented, measurable, long-term public health consequences as a result of that loss. This paper presents a forensic case for the federal enumeration of the bereaved parent demographic as a standard annual public health data collection. The United States bereaved parent population is estimated at 18.7 million individuals (Evermore, 2022), with independent corroboration from the Center for Advanced Pain Studies at the University of Texas at Austin (2026). This population carries documented elevated mortality risk, psychiatric hospitalization risk, marital disruption, workforce productivity loss, and long-term health system burden-all measurable, all consequential, and none currently tracked in any federal data system. The absence of a federal count is not a data limitation. It is a data gap-the result of a framing failure in which bereaved parents have been classified as a grief population requiring service delivery rather than a public health demographic requiring enumeration. This paper presents the evidentiary case for reclassification and formal federal counting.

title: Provincial Disparities in Child Stunting in Cambodia: A Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial Analysis, 2005–2021–22
affiliations: Ajou University School of Medicine and Ajou University School of Medicine

detail.title: Provincial Disparities in Child Stunting in Cambodia: A Bayesian Hierarchical Spatial Analysis, 2005–2021–22

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.

detail.abstract:
Background: Despite significant national progress in child health, stunting remains a major public health challenge in Cambodia, as national averages often mask substantial subnational variations. This study aimed to examine provincial disparities in child stunting trends in Cambodia from 2005 to 2021–22.

Methods: We analysed data from children younger than 5 years from four Cambodia Demographic and Health Surveys conducted in 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2021–22. We employed a Bayesian hierarchical spatial model with a Besag–York–Mollié 2 structure to analyse province-year aggregated data, adjusting for child, maternal, household, and water, sanitation, and hygiene-related covariates. We estimated model-based fitted prevalence, prevalence differences relative to Phnom Penh, and average annual percentage changes.

Findings: National stunting prevalence declined from 43·91% in 2005 to 23·34% in 2021–22. However, marked provincial disparities persisted throughout the study period. Compared with Phnom Penh, a high burden remained in provinces including Ratanak Kiri, Stung Treng, and Preah Vihear. The fastest improvements were observed in Banteay Meanchey and Battambang. These findings indicate that both the remaining burden and the pace of improvement were geographically uneven.

Interpretation: Although Cambodia achieved a marked reduction in child stunting, provincial inequalities remained. Province-specific monitoring and geographically targeted nutrition and development strategies are needed to address persistent inequalities in child nutrition.

title: Children missed by routine vaccination in India: interpretable neural networks and logistic regression for zero-dose and dropout
affiliations: Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi, University of Montreal and Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Delhi

detail.title: Children missed by routine vaccination in India: interpretable neural networks and logistic regression for zero-dose and dropout

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) [Grant/Award number: 40434].

detail.abstract: BackgroundReaching zero-dose children, defined here as children who have not received a first DTP-containing dose, is a global priority. However, zero-dose counts do not capture children who start vaccination and later drop out. In India, many children remain under-immunised, meaning that they miss one or more routine vaccine doses. We assessed whether the risk profile differs between non-initiation and later dropout, across geography, and beyond what additive regression can represent.Methods We analysed NFHS-5 child records for three outcomes: zero-dose (43{,}181 children; 2{,}976 positive), within-series dropout (DTP1--DTP3), defined as failure to complete the three-dose DTP-containing series after initiation (40{,}186; 2{,}578 positive), and cross-series dropout (BCG--MCV1), defined as receipt of BCG but not a first measles-containing vaccine dose across the first-year schedule (40{,}985; 3{,}510 positive). We fitted penalised logistic regression and feed-forward neural networks at pooled India, five macro-regions, and state level. To compare additive and non-additive risk structure, we used Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and interaction analyses.FindingsAt pooled India level, the neural network improved accuracy and Macro-F1 for all three outcomes; the largest gain was for cross-series dropout (BCG--MCV1). On a common SHAP scale, zero-dose risk was driven more strongly by deprivation, home delivery, and rural residence, whereas the two dropout outcomes gave greater weight to child age, birth order, and maternal educational disadvantage. Interaction analyses showed moderate non-additive structure centred on deprivation, maternal education, birth order, and service-contact variables. Regionally, Macro-F1 improved in all 15 region-outcome cells. At state level, mean gains remained positive, but minority-class detection was inconsistent; the main contribution at that scale was localisation of heterogeneous drivers and interaction pairs.InterpretationChildhood under-immunisation in India is not a single process. The risk profile differs between children who never start routine vaccination and those who start but do not complete it, and it varies across regions and states. Flexible models added value mainly by clarifying that structure rather than by simple algorithmic superiority.

title: Beyond Real Options: When Is Valuation under the Real-World Measure Arbitrage-Free?
affiliations: University of Wuppertal and Ampega Asset Management GmbH

detail.title: Beyond Real Options: When Is Valuation under the Real-World Measure Arbitrage-Free?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This paper reflects only the authors’ personal opinions and does not necessarily represent the views of the companies with which they are affiliated. The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare that are relevant to the content of this article.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces a unified arbitrage-free framework that links real-world expectations to risk-neutral valuation. We incorporate valuation under the real-world measure into the standard risk-neutral pricing paradigm and extend it to general contingent claims, deriving closed-form representations for certainty equivalents and risk-adjusted discount rates. 

Within this setting, we show that the traditional discounted cash flow (DCF) method emerges as a special case of arbitrage-free valuation under the real-world measure and is valid only for payoff structures that are linear in the numéraire return. For non-linear claims, including but not limited to investments containing real options, standard beta-based discounting is generally inconsistent with arbitrage-free pricing and can induce economically material mispricing.

More broadly, the framework clarifies the conceptual relationships among risk-neutral valuation, pricing kernels, certainty equivalents, and cost-of-capital approaches within a unified theoretical model. It also provides a precise characterization of the conditions under which real-world valuation methods remain consistent with arbitrage-free pricing.

title: The Sisyphean Pursuit of Evidence for Poverty Traps
affiliations: Northwestern University,  and Northwestern University

detail.title: The Sisyphean Pursuit of Evidence for Poverty Traps
detail.abstract:
Much of development economics, both micro and macro, posits theories and explores the empirics of poverty traps. A common theory centers around asset-threshold poverty traps in which marginal returns to capital increase sharply over a certain threshold and financial markets are incomplete. This combination leads households above this threshold to prosper while those below continuously fall back, trapped in poverty. Yet in economics, as best as we can tell, far more papers assume such thresholds than empirically demonstrate them. In a key recent exception, Balboni et al. (2022) (hereinafter “BBBGH”) argues that data from Bangladesh identifies clear evidence of such a threshold at slightly above the cost of a cow for recent recipients of a big push transfer program. We apply this analysis to data from seven other similar programs in low-income countries and find no evidence of an asset-threshold poverty trap. We then return to BBBGH and argue that their data do not support the identification of a poverty trap, with the point of disagreement being a log-transformation challenge and a potential geographic confound. In long-term representative rural panel data from Bangladesh and Ghana we find no evidence of divergence away from any particular threshold. While the threshold theory is undoubtedly true for some households, we argue that the pursuit of clear evidence of an asset-threshold poverty trap for a broad population is likely an aspirational goal rendered unachievable by the intersection of a multitude of possible mechanisms as well as heterogeneous agents.
